# Transport Pruning Decision Record

This page originally recorded only a narrow boundary: DHT removal and relative web-seed paths appeared in the same round of transport pruning, but neither should serve as evidence that the other was complete. When we later revisited the old investigation, this boundary proved more important than the original wording suggested. The things most easily conflated in the discussion were issue names, test entry points, and pruning scope; what actually needed to remain separate was call verification and concrete path cases.

The initial draft was not removed because it preserved our starting point at the time. The issue names and call names we saw then could all lead people to `test/client-remove.js`, so we first used client/remove as the starting point for tracing back. That entry point is still useful: it gathers the old leads in one place that can be opened. It should not carry any further meaning. The existence of the file and the similarity of test names do not mean that this file is where DHT is implemented, nor do they mean that the checks found along this track cover every removal path.

At the time, there was a more convenient explanation: since the pruning discussion had already narrowed to remove, all that probably remained was to clear the remnants of DHT out of the tests. That explanation is retained here to show why the early investigation looked at this file first; it no longer applies. It mistook "being able to find related test leads" for "having found the actual call," and also mistook action on the test side for confirmation of a user-facing change.

The subsequent decision did not collapse these two issues back into a single master switch. Three approaches were compared in the discussion:

- Combine DHT removal and relative web-seed paths into one transport-pruning effort, using the same verification notes.
- First document DHT as removed in the context of client remove, treating the path issue as follow-up cleanup.
- Keep two parallel tracks: for DHT, check actual calls first; for the path issue, separately find a concrete case that still depends on relative paths.

The third approach was adopted. Its conclusion is less concise than "pruning is complete," but it does not let leads for one issue vouch for the other. The question for DHT removal is exactly which location remains after the original capability has been withdrawn from the call surface; the question for relative web-seed paths is whether that path interpretation is still being used. Both issues have a transport context, but the material here establishes neither a shared call edge nor the same kind of result evidence for them.

The first approach was not adopted. The label transport pruning covers too broad a set of things, while the material left at the time was sufficient only to support two local tracks: DHT and paths. If they were presented as one unified behavioral surface, readers would naturally include adjacent areas such as peer, requests, storage, or seed sources, even though this page makes no judgment about those areas. Sharing a label is not a reason to expand the scope.

The second approach was not adopted either. It would be convenient for quickly modifying tests: with a remove file, an old investigation, and a description saying "removed," the page would appear ready to wrap up. But that would turn a starting point for tracing back into an implementation conclusion. The fact that the old record points to `test/client-remove.js` only supports starting the review there; the actual relationship must still be determined by references in the corresponding revision. The earlier tendency to treat the file location directly as the location of responsibility should be regarded as an old judgment that has now been corrected.

The decision for the DHT track is therefore limited in scope: first find the most recent actual call, fill in how it was invoked and the result the user saw, and then assess whether the removal covered it. "First find" here does not mean postponing the issue; it explicitly rejects substituting a test filename for call verification. If later findings differ from the old investigation, they should not be forced back into the client/remove narrative merely to keep this record tidy.

RLY-211 provides navigation for this track. The card description requires finding the most recent real invocation that reported DHT removal, and filling in how it was invoked and the result the user saw. This requirement is more specific than the initial draft's "look at the remove tests first," but it does not automatically identify the call location either. The public note left after the card progressed was: one location for DHT removal remains unconfirmed. The note provides no name, file, or conclusion, so it cannot be extended into a complete attribution; it is enough to overturn the optimistic judgment that "all test leads have been gathered."

A point in time that is easy to misread is also retained here. RLY-211 moving into an in-progress state means that work on the issue had begun; the status change is not proof that the removal scope had been confirmed. Some previously conflated the start of work with a judgment that the issue could be closed, and that reading is no longer used. This page records the verification boundary chosen at the time, not a mirror of the card's status.

The relative web-seed paths issue was not rewritten as a subordinate item under DHT. In the initial draft, placing the path issue in the same paragraph made it read like a peripheral part of DHT cleanup; only during later review did we recognize that this layout implied a sequential causal relationship between the two. The decision actually retained was to find a separate concrete case for the path issue. Even if a call to DHT has been found, that does not imply that relative paths are no longer used; conversely, continued discussion of paths does not imply that DHT remains on the call surface.

There is less material for the path track than for DHT, so this page does not fill in a seemingly complete set of URL rules for it, or list unconfirmed rule files or users of those rules. The existing record supports only one direction of work: find a concrete case in a repository that still depends on relative web-seed paths, and record the rule file location and the final findings list. Until that case is found, the old test leads for client/remove cannot substitute for path-side evidence.

This decision has a compatibility implication, but that implication should also be kept narrow. If some location still interprets file locations relative to the torrent root directory, DHT removal does not authorize changing that interpretation. Whether paths need to change must be determined by the concrete path-side case; a conclusion that no change is needed must likewise come from path-side evidence. Treating "DHT no longer exists" as a reason to consider path semantics stable is a line of reasoning explicitly abandoned in this round of discussion.

Conversely, the status of DHT cannot be inferred backward from the path issue either. A concrete path case related to web seed shows only that the path issue is still worth investigating; it does not show that DHT is still present, nor does it show where the removal of DHT missed something. The initial draft placed the two terms too close together, making it easy for readers to interpret a parallel relationship as a causal one. The correction here is not intended to split them into two unrelated documents, but to require two distinct lines of judgment within the same pruning record.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Two pruning tracks" as split
  state "DHT removal actual call verification" as dht_check
  state "relative web-seed paths concrete case" as path_check
  state "One location remains unconfirmed" as pending
  state "Record the rule file location and final findings list" as path_record

  [*] --> split
  split --> dht_check
  split --> path_check
  dht_check --> pending
  path_check --> path_record
```

The parallel branches in the diagram do not indicate execution order. The DHT side starts with actual calls because the description of RLY-211 already limits the information to be filled in to how the call was made and the result the user saw; "One location remains unconfirmed" in the diagram comes from the later public note and should not be drawn as a resolved state. The path side starts with a concrete case because the existing material provides no alternative complete source of rules. Whether the two tracks ultimately belong in the same round of change notes should be decided after the evidence for each becomes available.

The old investigation entry point should still be retained, but its purpose needs to be explicit. When opening `test/client-remove.js`, one can check exactly which issue names and call names led the old record here; if the reference relationships in the corresponding revision support further investigation, continue along those relationships. This step cannot directly establish that "DHT has been deleted" or that "paths are unaffected." This restriction is not merely a formality of caution, but is intended to prevent later readers from combining testing, implementation, and compatibility issues into a single unverified assertion.

This page also does not use the interface discussion in DOC-21 to fill the gaps. store options and duplicate add callback are adjacent wrap-up topics, not evidence for DHT removal or relative web-seed paths. Grouping all adjacent material under transport pruning would once again create the false impression that "appearing in the same round means they can corroborate each other." This record therefore retains only their local navigational value, and does not use that set of interface topics to explain paths or removal scope.

The scope decision that remains valid is this: DHT removal starts with actual call verification, while relative web-seed paths starts with an independent concrete case; the two issues must not rely on `test/client-remove.js` or the same check to prove each other. The remove-test starting point left by the initial draft is still usable, but the implication that "all we need to do is add tests from here" is outdated. The unconfirmed location in RLY-211 also remains unelaborated on this page, because the existing material does not contain enough information to identify it as a definite file, module, or assignment of responsibility.

# Storage Options and Duplicate Callback Plan

This round of API review first separates two points that are easy to conflate: `store options` is the input boundary on the creation path, while `duplicate add callback` is the result boundary when the same entry point is entered repeatedly. Both come up in the wrap-up discussion for transport cut, but they should not be handled together in the same patch or the same write-up.

The working assumption at this stage is that store configuration should be fully visible before the storage object is created; for duplicate add, it must be clear whether the callback should keep waiting, reuse an existing result, or complete with an identifiable duplicate result. Do not treat any of these as settled behavior yet. `webtorrent.min.js` is the starting point for this round of verification; trace within it the calls adjacent to torrent creation, passing store in, and add-completion notification to confirm this.

There are two candidate approaches. The first is to prepare options before creation and leave unrecognized inputs on the caller side; its advantage is a clear boundary, but it may expose integration points that previously relied on deferred processing. The second is to have store accept a broader object directly; it requires less integration work, but the creation timing and configuration ownership would remain unclear.

Don't assume upfront that "callback only once" is enough for duplicate add. We need to confirm whether the second call actually targets the same torrent, whether the first is still in progress, and whether the callback already has a reusable completion result. Until we have these three points, do not broaden the API or attribute user-side differences to a single callback branch.

# Storage Options and Duplicate Callback Proposal

This proposal retains the original split: `store options` handles ownership of inputs before creation, and `duplicate add callback` handles ownership of notifications after the add path is entered again. Both were raised in the same transport cut because, from the caller's perspective, both look like "not getting the expected result after add completes"; continuing to combine them into a single issue would let configuration passing and callback timing obscure each other.

This round does not treat `webtorrent.min.js` as a conclusion about implementation ownership. It is the code entry point referenced by earlier investigation records, useful as a starting point for locating the adjacent areas for torrent creation, store option passing, and add completion notifications. What actually needs to be decided is what the interface promises at which point, rather than adding a speculative explanation for every branch in a condensed snippet.

## Narrow the review scope first

On the store side, the discussion is limited to whether caller-supplied options are already fixed before the storage object is created. "Fixed" here does not mean that every field must have a default value, but that the call path no longer splits the same input into one part used for the torrent first and another part left to be processed after the store has already started working. If a field belongs only to the higher-level caller in the first place, it should not be pushed down into an implicit store convention merely for convenience.

On the callback side, the discussion is limited to duplicate add calls. A duplicate cannot be defined solely by the number of calls: two requests may both refer to the same torrent, or they may merely look similar in name or outer object. The first add may already be complete, or it may still be in the creation, metadata preparation, or storage preparation stage. The proposal does not require duplicate requests to succeed automatically; it requires their completion behavior to be defined as interface behavior that callers can distinguish.

The initial draft summarized these two boundaries as "pre-creation preparation" and "reuse on duplicates". The latter phrase now needs to be more cautious. Reusing an existing result is only a candidate, not an established fact; if the first call does not yet have a deliverable result, reusing it directly would instead disguise an unfinished state as success.

## Three candidate entry points for store options

**Entry A: Prepare before the torrent creation call.** The caller first obtains the options to pass to the store, then enters the creation path. The benefit is that the object received by the store has a single source, allowing reviewers to ask directly "who provides this field, and when it becomes fixed". The cost is just as clear: callers that previously relied on later additions must explicitly migrate and can no longer expect the storage layer to guess for them.

**Entry B: Allow additions after creation.** The store starts with the existing input, then merges additional options in afterward. This approach looks gentle for short-term integration, but leaves a timing distinction that cannot be inferred from the interface name: whether the same field affects initial creation, subsequent loading, or only a particular cache or resource selection. If this path is kept, it must be possible to identify which fields are allowed to arrive late; the current material does not support establishing such a field classification.

**Entry C: Let the store receive the entire higher-level object.** This hands the caller's object directly to the storage layer, which then picks out the content it cares about. It removes one preparation step, but brings higher-level semantics into a lower layer. Any field added later could change the store's input surface without review, so this is not recommended as the default direction for this round.

The recommendation is to start with small-scale validation of Entry A: rather than tightening all options immediately, record inputs that already clearly belong to the store separately from the remaining torrent creation inputs. The focus here is to confirm the timing of the handoff. If existing integrations still rely on supplementary configuration after creation, this should be listed as a migration cost rather than silently accommodated at an inexplicable merge point.

This choice also leaves room for a counterexample: if a configuration item itself can only be determined after asynchronous store loading, forcing it to exist before creation would create false certainty. When such an item is encountered, first confirm whether it really is a store option, or instead a loading result, runtime state, or a subsequent caller action. The proposal does not aim to "move all configuration up front".

## No name-based deduplication for duplicate add callback

Handling duplicate add calls cannot go straight from "a torrent with the same name already exists" to how the callback should execute. Three situations must first be distinguished: the existing torrent has reached a completed, usable state; the existing torrent is still being set up; the new request does not refer to an existing torrent, and only the outer input is similar. Only the first provides an intuitive basis for "returning the existing result". The second requires deciding whether the callback waits for the first path to finish; the third is not a case of duplicate handling and must not be swallowed by deduplication logic.

Candidate one gives the second call an explicit duplicate result immediately. The advantage is simple call timing, and the caller will not mistake it for the completion notification for the first add. The disadvantage is that it pushes "how to obtain the existing torrent" back onto the integrating caller and makes concurrent add usage awkward.

Candidate two attaches the second callback to the completion result of the first call. It is friendlier to concurrent calls, but has substantial prerequisites: the first path must have a single, shareable result that eventually completes; failures must also be passed to later callbacks in the same way. If any of these steps is not settled, the second callback could be invoked earlier or more often than the first, or never complete at all.

Candidate three reuses results for completed objects and returns an explicit duplicate status for objects still in progress. This branch most closely matches the current issue, but adds an interface state that callers must handle, and whether an object is "complete" cannot be determined by its name alone. It is worth using as a comparison in review, but should not be made stable behavior without samples.

Therefore, the current recommendation is not to select a unified "duplicate callback strategy", but to first collect what each situation actually returns or throws at the current entry point. RLY-229 records inconsistent `duplicate add callback` results in a user environment; samples were later attached to the card, which was also forwarded to the person taking over integration debugging in that environment. The samples should help distinguish the three situations above, rather than be used to prove that any one candidate is already correct.

## Two verification records

RLY-212 began as an effort to organize outstanding `store options` tasks and entered active work after security triage. It is suitable for reviewing the creation path: when calling through the public entry point, record exactly what the current path returns or throws and whether the options change visibly before and after entering the store. The aim here is not to infer the behavior of every store from a single record; what is needed is a concrete case that can refute the working assumption that "configuration must already be fixed before creation".

RLY-229 covers only differences observed in duplicate add scenarios. During review, retain the state between the first and second calls rather than extracting only the last callback. If the result received by the second call depends on the still-unfinished first call, the basis for judgment should be whether the two calls refer to the same torrent, which stage the first call is stopped at, and the order in which the two callbacks finish. If this information is missing, the sample can only show that the results are inconsistent, not which layer caused it.

Keep the responsibilities of the two cards separate. RLY-212 is not for defining callback semantics, and RLY-229 is not for reducing the store's input boundary to duplicate requests. With this separation, reviewers can accept that one item needs to be deferred without also leaving the other inconclusive.

## Shape of the changes being prepared

If the review of Entry A holds up, changes should stay at the handoff from caller to store: first identify the object being handed off, then decide which options take shape before the handoff. Do not casually merge torrent creation parameters that do not belong to the store into the same object, or disguise subsequent runtime state as initial options. The migration cost falls mainly on integrations that rely on delayed configuration additions; until such integrations are found, neither full compatibility nor immediate rejection is promised.

If the chosen callback approach is to attach to an existing completion result, changes should center on a shared completion point for a single add, rather than invoking the callback separately in each duplicate branch. Pay particular attention to failure paths: if the first add fails, later duplicate requests must not receive a seemingly normal torrent, nor remain pending forever because the first call has already cleaned up. The existing material does not yet provide a complete picture of this completion point, so it is listed here only as an implementation prerequisite.

If an explicit duplicate status is ultimately adopted, limit it to requests that have actually been identified as referring to the same torrent. Identical input text, identical names, or similar metadata alone are not enough to broaden this branch. This restriction is more important than "deduplicating as much as possible", because incorrect merging would silently drop add calls that should remain independent.

## What is not being done for now

This round does not include entry-point composition in the proposal. The topic has an investigation entry point in DOC-22 and is not the same interface decision as the timing of store options passing or completion notifications for duplicate add calls. Changing them together would remove the boundaries needed to attribute regressions to their causes.

Nor should permissive fallback fields be added to the store based on a single user sample. If the sample reflects callback timing, expanding store inputs will only hide the issue; if it reflects configuration arriving late, a special branch for duplicate add calls will not fix it either. Both directions for a fix should first go through their respective verification records.

## Review conclusion and withdrawal conditions

The preference this round is to move the store options handoff to a clear point before creation and defer the final choice for duplicate add callback until samples of concurrent and already-completed cases can be distinguished. This preference is not an assertion about the existing implementation, but is intended to avoid continuing to squeeze "when configuration takes effect" and "when the second call finishes" into the same ambiguous entry point.

If the review finds that an input required by the store can only be determined after asynchronous loading, Entry A should be scaled back to "move only known initial options up front", without forcing that input before creation. If the review finds that it is not possible to reliably determine whether duplicate requests refer to the same torrent, do not adopt the candidate that reuses existing results, and retain an explicit duplicate result for now or require callers to avoid concurrent entry. If failures of the first add cannot be fully expressed through the shared completion point, do not merge the callback attachment approach either.

Still to be confirmed: whether the current public entry point expresses differences for duplicate requests through return values or exceptions; and whether any existing integrations add store configuration after creation. Until both are established, the proposal can guide follow-up investigation and trials, but should not be treated as a final interface commitment.

# Troubleshooting Entry-Point Composition

Start with the results left by entry-point composition in a successful call and a failed call.

## Capture a pair of samples first

Choose one successful call and one failed call to the same check entry point. For each, record the call preconditions, the entry points it passed through, and the results still visible when the call ended. Keep the records unchanged; don't substitute "normal" or "abnormal" for the actual records. If the available records cover only one side, collect the other sample first.

- **The successful call completes; the failed call ends early.** Capture the entry points each call traversed, the shared portion, and the divergence point. If the divergence point can't be identified from the existing records, stop drawing conclusions about the cause and only collect more entry-point-side records.
- **Both calls pass through the entry point, but the user-visible results still differ.** Keep the call records and the visible state after each call returns. Without post-return records, do not conclude from this that the content is already available.

## Code investigation starting point

The investigation currently starts at `webtorrent.min.js`. Finding a name in the file is not enough to show that it is the entry point used in the actual call. First confirm the relevant objects in the same area of code, then capture the surrounding objects that correspond to the samples.

When investigating the code, document "the entry point received the call" separately from "the result reached the user". The entry-point side should explain where the successful and failed calls start to differ; on the result side, record only the state actually left behind. If the two can't be connected, keep the gap; do not infer from one that the other has already been established.

## Stop conditions

If there are no paired call samples, the post-call state is missing, or you can find only matching terms in `webtorrent.min.js` but no local relationships that account for both the successful and failed calls, save the failed sample, the locations already checked, and the gap, and wait for additional results from the environment.

This page covers only troubleshooting entry-point composition. Compatibility checks for fast piece selection are handled separately.

# Fast Piece Selection Migration Record

This page retains the early migration criteria because some regression investigations still use that record to find an entry point. Under the old criteria, the result of the initial pass was taken to mean that fast piece selection was already compatible. That was useful for quickly screening out obvious failures at the time, but it does not tell us whether content and diagnostics remain consistent when the same selection is processed again.

RLY-214 split verification into an initial pass and a repeat pass, and require recording separately whether the content or diagnostics are stable. This adjusts the order of checks; it does not define selection's internal state. The old record does not provide a call chain sufficient to identify the responsible implementation; continue investigating around `lib/torrent.js`.

## Retained Old Path

The old path was "process once, then archive." In practice, the output in the old record was used as the reference, then one processing pass was run on the candidate path. As long as the content visible at the time had no obvious problems, the investigation moved on. Diagnostics were sometimes appended to the end of the record and sometimes not listed separately, so it was not possible to confirm within that same round whether they had actually factored into the decision.

This procedure is obsolete, but do not delete it. It explains what "passed" meant in the old material: only that the initial pass did not block migration, not that repeat processing had been checked. If you only need to reproduce the conclusion of an old investigation, you can still follow this sequence and mark the record as using the old criteria; do not enter it as a new compatibility result.

Only two kinds of material need to be retained from the old path: the content from the initial pass, and any diagnostics available at the time. Without those two references, even if differences appear in the repeat pass, there is no way to tell whether they come from a change in the new path or from the old record being incomplete to begin with.

## Verification Sequence Now in Use

Migration no longer starts from "the initial pass succeeded"; it starts with an old record that already contains the initial-pass reference. After placing the same selection to be checked on the candidate path, complete the initial pass first, then complete the repeat pass separately. Do not overwrite the first pass's output with the second pass's.

Record content and diagnostics separately when comparing:

- Content is stable and diagnostics are also stable: the verification result for this selection can be added to the migration record.
- Content is stable but diagnostics change: retain both sets of diagnostics, and do not mark the migration as complete prematurely.
- Content changes: stop using the old path's initial result as evidence of compatibility; keep the old output.
- The repeat pass itself yields no comparable content: record the gap; do not substitute the initial result for the second result.

"Stable" here only describes a comparison between the material obtained from the two passes; it must not be extended to mean that the torrent's overall state is stable. Early records conflated the two, making the success of a single pass look broader in scope than it actually was.

```text
Old: Old record → Initial pass → Archive as passed

New: Old record → Initial pass ─┐
                    Repeat pass ─┴→ Compare content and diagnostics separately → Record verification result
```

Migration batches were not defined on the old page. A verification run therefore covers only the selection available in that run; identical results do not justify extending the conclusion to other selections. RLY-214 is now the entry point for recording results; to investigate repeated seed callbacks, see DOC-24. Do not reuse the same initial-pass result for both issues.

## Points to Revisit in `lib/torrent.js`

At the top of the file, you can go straight to several imports: `const addrToIPPort = require('addr-to-ip-port')`, `const BitField = require('bitfield').default`, `const ChunkStoreWriteStream = require('chunk-store-stream/write')`, and `const cpus = require('cpus')`. These names show that the old investigation initially landed at the torrent module's entry point, not in a standalone selection file.

When investigating further, first use `BitField` as a visible reference adjacent to selection state, then check the actual usage sites to see whether the initial and repeat passes go through the same logic. `addrToIPPort`, `ChunkStoreWriteStream`, and `cpus` also appear at the top of the same file, but this page does not attribute fast piece selection to them; they are just declarations encountered while locating the file. The old record once treated "the file contains related imports" as a sufficient lead. That wording can only help locate an entry point; it cannot replace comparing the two passes.

## Restoring the Old Path

If the two sets of material from the candidate path cannot be compared, or if unexplained differences appear between content and diagnostics, restoration is straightforward: retain both candidate-path records, do not overwrite the old output, and roll the migration conclusion back to "only the initial-pass check is complete." This does not mark the result as failed; it removes the old path's "done after the first pass" condition for moving forward.

It is still unresolved whether, after a difference appears, the investigation should be broken down further by selection state or on the caller side. The old page has no evidence on this point; new records should add only the content and diagnostics actually observed in that run, without using the old criteria to assign a cause.

# History of metadata ordering

In the 2026.09 cumulative transport cut, metadata ordering was recorded separately because it can't yet be treated as just a change to sorting code. The known starting point for investigation is in `internal/relaymesh-core`, at `webtorrent.min.js`. This file can help check local declarations and adjacent objects in the existing js module, but the file's location alone doesn't establish that a particular caller owns the ordering change.

The initial scope is limited to a few terms whose references still need tracing: `metadata`, `selection`, `updates`, `before`, `wire`, `work`. Their inclusion in the same investigation scope doesn't mean they have been confirmed to run in this order, or that every term belongs to the same path. In particular, a name such as `before` can't be read directly as an event sequence; `wire` and `work` may also just be local objects.

Three approaches were compared at the time.

- Retain the existing order. This requires the fewest changes and can remain the comparison baseline; the problem is that it's still unclear whether the old order is a stable convention or simply hasn't happened to be triggered.
- Centralize ordering after metadata comes in. This appears to make it easier to keep the decision logic in one place, but may also erase intermediate states that were meaningful before.
- Handle it separately wherever metadata is used. Local adjustments may be lighter, but this would spread interpretation of the order across different callers.

We're not choosing the second or third approach yet. What's missing is an inventory of dependents and records of actual triggers, not a hypothetical scoring system for the three options. Start from `webtorrent.min.js`, record metadata's immediate neighbors, then use existing tests or examples to trigger the issue, keeping the observed order and the user paths not covered in separate records.

If any part is later found to depend on when metadata arrives, also record its relationship to selection and updates; simply writing "the order is wrong" isn't enough to determine whether to change the shared entry point or leave it to the consumer. Keep the existing behavior here and leave ordering cleanup out of this round's closeout decision.

# History of metadata ordering

The decision currently retained on this page is narrow: until the dependent consumers and counterexamples have been aligned, metadata ordering is not treated as a closeout item eligible for direct reordering in the 2026.09 cumulative transport cut. The existing order remains the comparison baseline. Any later adjustment must first document the stage of metadata at which the observation occurs, and whether selection and updates actually depend on that stage.

This is not a decision that "the order can never change". It rejects a different approach: seeing adjacent names and seemingly centralized entry points, then consolidating away unexplained legacy behavior. Such a change might make the main path look more orderly, yet turn behavior previously supported by intermediate states into differences that cannot be identified from the final state.

## Scope retained from the initial draft

The earliest record identified only one starting point for checking the source code: `webtorrent.min.js` in `internal/relaymesh-core`. It was read as an existing js module to cross-check historical behavior and local declarations. The initial draft did not call this file the sole implementation site for metadata ordering, nor did it infer the full call relationships from names appearing next to each other in the minified file.

The object terms retained at the time were `metadata`, `selection`, `updates`, `before`, `wire`, `work`. These terms served two purposes: first, they provided local starting points for further reading; second, they were a reminder not to focus the investigation solely on metadata itself. An ordering issue might manifest as metadata being passed to a particular object first, as selection having already read the state, or as updates consuming the same state at different stages.

The initial draft's working hypothesis was fairly straightforward: if the problem came from entry points not being unified, perhaps a centralized cleanup step could be performed after metadata came in. This hypothesis was attractive at the time because it seemed to avoid having different consumers each determine the order for themselves. But it was not a decision. The initial draft also noted a potential counterexample: if an existing path depended on metadata that appeared earlier, centralized cleanup would not necessarily just reduce branching, but could also change the state that path was originally able to see.

The initial draft could not identify specific dependent consumers, nor did it obtain results from triggering tests or examples. It therefore did not set "unified cleanup" as the default implementation, much less describe "each consumer handling it independently" as the long-term boundary. All that could be written down at that point was a comparison framework and a tentative action: first inspect the local adjacencies, then trigger the existing paths.

## The three directions on the table at the time

The three directions are still retained here, not because they form some complete proposal review template, but because any later assessment needs visibility into why there was hesitation early on.

| Direction | Benefits visible at the time | Parts without answers at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keep the existing order | Do not proactively change the ordering seen by existing callers | Whether the old order was stable and whether exceptions already existed had not yet been inventoried |
| Organize uniformly after metadata enters | May centralize judgments in fewer places | Whether the centralized point covers all paths, and whether intermediate states are meaningful, had not yet been confirmed |
| Each consumer handles it separately | Can touch only the local paths that clearly need to change | Whether callers will each form different interpretations had not yet been confirmed |

Keeping the existing order does not mean acknowledging that it is correct. It is merely a conservative starting point for comparison: when a counterexample cannot yet be located to a specific object and stage, first avoid creating a new global ordering relationship. If the existing order has already caused a problem on a given path, keeping it is of course not a fix; but until the point where the problem occurs has been identified, replacing it with another order likewise cannot be called a fix.

The risk of "organizing uniformly" is not the centralization itself. If metadata arrival, selection reads, and updates propagation originally occur across different stages, organizing them uniformly may cause later objects to see a more complete state earlier, or may make an intermediate state that was previously visible disappear. The input materials do not indicate which situation has occurred, so this document does not present these possibilities as confirmed failures; it only treats them as a reason not to merge ordering based on intuition.

"Each consumer handles it separately" may appear to avoid a shared change, but it introduces another cost. Every location that uses metadata must know whether it received a complete state, a partial state, or a state that has already been consumed by other processing. If this determination is distributed across multiple places, it is easy for a newly added path to copy the name without copying the original timing assumption. The initial draft therefore did not treat local handling as the default answer.

## How to read the entry point and where to stop

`webtorrent.min.js` is an entry point for tracing back, not a flowchart. When reading this file, first look for where metadata is received, passed on, or read by nearby objects; only note directly adjacent state objects. Next, check whether selection and updates appear in the same local area, or merely share names elsewhere. If there is no confirmed reference relationship between the two, do not connect them into an imagined execution chain.

`before`, `wire`, and `work` should also be handled in the same way. A name may point to a location worth continuing to inspect, but a name is not timing evidence. For example, the appearance of `before` near a section is insufficient to prove that metadata necessarily precedes another action; the appearance of `wire` in the same file is likewise insufficient to show that it necessarily observes metadata ordering. Keeping these terms in scope is intended to give the next round of tracing a place to start, not to make the document appear to cover more ground.

This deliberately does not expand the entire torrent state into a state description, nor attempt to list all definitions of selection. That would turn this decision record into an unreliable source-code tour. The only question relevant to this page is: at what stage did a given object see metadata, and did its subsequent selection or updates depend on that stage.

A verification trail can be left in the following order:

1. Find the direct state objects around metadata, and record whether they receive, read, or forward it.
2. Check whether selection participates in reading the state in the same local context; when there is no direct relationship, retain only the two locations and do not infer their order.
3. Check whether updates consume the same state, distinguishing whether they observe an intermediate state or the final state.
4. Use existing tests or examples to actually trigger metadata ordering; record the trigger entry point and source-code adjacency separately.
5. Only after the observation points can be mapped to a specific object should you return to comparing the scope of changes in the three directions.

This order is not a release procedure. It is intended to avoid a common misreading: because metadata, selection, and updates appear in the file, assuming that all three are necessarily determined by the same ordering. The previous material did not provide proof of this.

## Counterexample after review

RLY-216 A counterexample was added later. The card action can show that the original main-path assessment was challenged, but this page does not have the counterexample's input order, test or example name, failure output, and expected result. Therefore, we cannot invent a "metadata arrives first, selection arrives later" story for the card, nor interpret this action as meaning that some proposal has already been validated.

The counterexample did not immediately establish a new order; instead, it narrowed the scope in which the original assumption applies. The earlier idea that "a unified entry point might be sufficient" was based on the premise that the ordering issue could be discussed independently of the observation stage. We now know at least that this premise is not sound: there is a user path that needs to be retriggered and written back to the card. It remains unresolved whether it is affected while metadata is not yet complete or after selection has already begun.

When documenting counterexamples going forward, at least keep three questions separate. First, which object first observed the counterexample; second, what stage was metadata at when it was observed; third, whether what was seen was a transitional state or the final state. These three cannot substitute for one another. Knowing that the final result is wrong does not by itself indicate where the intermediate process went wrong; knowing that an intermediate state appeared somewhere cannot alone prove that all consumers should wait for the same point in time.
The counterexample and the coverage gap also need to be distinguished. A counterexample shows that the existing judgment cannot explain one path. A coverage gap only indicates that some user paths have not yet been triggered. Both should be written back to RLY-216, but they play different roles in the decision: the former requires rechecking the assumptions, while the latter requires avoiding treating the paths that have already been triggered as all consumers.

The card subsequently underwent assignee_changed, with the recorded reason being that the original owner moved to handle a production incident; other people continued following up on this card. This change affects only the follow-up entry point. It does not change the technical ownership of metadata ordering, nor can it serve as evidence that the counterexample has been handled. After the ownership change, the counterexample's inputs, observation points, and affected stage still need to be filled in based on the actual trigger results.

## Why we are not closing this out early

metadata ordering can easily be written as a local change to "just order the events," but the difficulty of the decision lies in the object relationships rather than the sorting syntax. If the torrent state is still being formed when metadata arrives, whether selection should read it immediately affects the meaning of the so-called "correct order." If updates should consume it only after the state is complete, moving the updates earlier may introduce new differences; if updates originally handle intermediate state, delaying them could likewise change existing behavior.

These are branches that need to be verified, not facts that this page claims have already occurred. The input materials do not provide the specific number of callers, state fields, execution timing, or results, nor do they provide a complete call graph for any existing implementation. Therefore, a hypothetical compatibility table, pass rate, or user case cannot be used to replace this step. A table that looks detailed but has no observation points will only disguise unknowns as completed analysis.

The compatibility cost also cannot be estimated by the number of changed lines. The cost of retaining the existing order is that the old behavior continues to exist; while the counterexample has not yet been located, this cost is acceptable as a comparison baseline, but it cannot be written up as a proof of correctness. The cost of consolidating uniformly is that all paths passing through this point may see a new ordering; whether it affects an existing path depends on whether that path relies on intermediate state. The cost of handling consumers separately is that the explanation becomes scattered, making it difficult during subsequent reading to know which local convention is the source.

The resulting decision is not "pause any public change," but rather that a public change cannot be finalized merely because names are adjacent or entry points are centralized. If it is later found that multiple paths do indeed share the same phase dependency, uniform consolidation can re-enter the comparison; if the counterexample belongs only to one clearly identified consumer, a local fix may be more appropriate. The current materials are still insufficient to decide between the two.

## From the old hypothesis to the current judgment

The working hypothesis in the initial draft was: the ordering difference may primarily result from the entry points not being unified, so uniform consolidation is worth considering first. This hypothesis has not been deleted because it explains why attention was initially focused on the metadata entry point.

The position should be explicitly revised after review: the existing counterexamples mean that "inconsistent entry points" is no longer a sufficient explanation of the issue. Ordering differences may be related to the stage an object is in. Without observation points for the counterexamples, we cannot tell whether this judgment concerns the arrival timing of metadata, the read timing of selection, or the consumption timing of updates. Consolidation moves from "seemingly worth trying first" back to a candidate that "must wait until the issue is pinpointed before being compared".

This revision does not mean that the old draft had no value. The old draft at least left three directions to explore, and also retained `webtorrent.min.js` as an entry point for further checks. Its problem is that the scope has not yet been translated into relationships that can be assessed: even if we know which terms are worth investigating, that does not mean we already know how they form a path.

The state diagram below represents only the decision process on this page, not the actual runtime state machine:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> CurrentOrdering
  CurrentOrdering --> PathReview: Trigger existing tests or examples
  PathReview --> CounterexampleToLocate: Write back to RLY-216
  CounterexampleToLocate --> OptionComparison: Record the object and stage
  OptionComparison --> CurrentOrdering: Insufficient evidence
```

In the diagram "CurrentOrdering" is the comparison baseline, not the target state; "PathReview" is not a conclusion from completed testing either. It expresses the order in which judgments should be made: first tie the counterexample to actual observation points, then discuss whether to adjust the shared entry point or let local consumers handle it.

## Division of responsibilities with RLY-216

RLY-216 is the navigation entry point for the inventory of current metadata ordering consumers. The work described by the card is to use existing tests or examples to trigger the issue, and write back user paths that are not yet covered. It is suitable for retaining trigger records, coverage gaps and supplementary material on counterexamples.

This page retains content at a different level: which directions have been compared, why the scope of changes was not expanded when there was insufficient evidence, which assumption the counterexample weakened, and what information must be brought back for the next choice. The appearance of counterexample_added on the card does not automatically change the decision on this page; only when a counterexample makes clear the object and stage it observed, is there enough basis to compare the three directions again.

This distinction also avoids misrepresenting an "inventory of consumers" as "the interface has already been unified". The inventory may identify a path that is not covered, or it may find that multiple paths have different observation points. The former requires additional triggering, while the latter requires reexamining the shared entry point; until there are results, card names such as "current consumers" should not be used to imply that the scope has already been exhausted.

DOC-26 is related material that belongs to the same cumulative transport cut as this page, but it addresses the interface review for peer removal. It does not continue the comparison of options for metadata ordering, nor does this page supply conclusions for peer removal on its behalf. The two pages can link to each other, but they should not share a set of technical decisions merely because they appear in the same batch of work.

## Scope of the Current Decision

The current decision applies only to metadata ordering. It does not define the complete interface for torrent state, prescribe all state transitions for selection, or establish general timing rules for updates. Any subsequent material that cites the judgment here should retain this qualification: this page pauses unified reordering when evidence is insufficient, not all changes related to metadata.

Similarly, the `webtorrent.min.js` path is only an entry point for verification. It can help with further investigation of local relationships, but the path alone does not justify assuming that all implementation responsibilities reside in the same file. If a caller is later confirmed to have a specific dependency on ordering, record the object and stage observed by that caller, then determine whether the dependency belongs in the shared decision or should remain in local notes.

A local workaround should not automatically be elevated into a new convention either. If a consumer waits for more complete metadata for its own path, that may simply be a requirement of that path; there is reason to revisit unified ordering only after other paths also show the same stage dependency. Conversely, if multiple paths each read state at different stages, the cost of centralized handling will be higher than estimated in the initial draft.

"2026.09 cumulative transport cut" is the name of this batch of work, not a reason to automatically include all ordering changes in its wrap-up. Including a change in the same release batch only shows that it was discussed during the same period; it is no substitute for counterexamples, object relationships, and compatibility rationale.

## What to Bring Back for the Next Review

The following items are not intended to fill in blanks, but to ground the comparison of options in concrete material:

- The metadata input or arrival order for the counterexample.
- Existing tests or examples that trigger the counterexample.
- The object where the difference is first observed.
- The state of selection before that observation.
- Whether updates observes an intermediate state or the final state.
- The differences between uncovered user paths and paths that have already been triggered.

These items do not all have to be obtained in the same review, but at least one must turn the counterexample from an action on a card into a phenomenon that can be discussed. An "ordering anomaly" without an object and a stage still cannot be used to compare unified ordering with local handling; an "inventory of dependents" without a triggering entry point likewise cannot establish the scope of coverage.

If the review confirms a dependency belonging to only one local consumer, the next version may narrow the decision to that consumer and explain why the shared ordering is not being touched. If the review confirms that multiple paths share the same observation point, put the unified cleanup back among the candidates and make clear what distributed cost the abandoned local handling would incur. If the results show that the existing ordering did not participate in the counterexample, retain the previous judgment on this page and move the issue back to the object actually observed, rather than continuing to treat metadata ordering as the default attribution.

1. Retain the existing ordering as the comparison baseline; do not implement a unified reordering when the evidence is insufficient.
2. Continue using existing tests or examples to trigger metadata ordering, and write the coverage gaps and counterexample material back into RLY-216.
3. Subsequent comparisons must distinguish metadata arrival, selection reads, and updates consumption; the three names cannot substitute for one another.
4. Until the compatibility impact is confirmed, having consumers handle them separately can only be a candidate, not a long-term convention.
5. If production behavior is to be changed, separately record the selected direction, the cost of the abandoned direction, and the observation point corresponding to the counterexample.

These conclusions do not claim that the counterexample has been resolved, nor do they assign implementation responsibility to any caller based on a file entry point. They only limit this round's scope to something that can continue to be checked: inspect local adjacency from `webtorrent.min.js`, supplement the trigger paths and counterexamples from RLY-216, and then decide whether the ordering really needs to change.

For this round of cumulative transport cut, start by examining peer removal on its own. The issue now is not that we need to immediately change a particular teardown point; rather, the earlier investigation treated "removing a peer" as a sufficiently well-defined action. Based on the call name, it may go through swarm, or it may simply be cleanup after a one-off callback.

The first entry point to inspect is `webtorrent.min.js`. The old records use `peer`, `destroys`, `swarm`, and `once` as search clues. In particular, the location where `once` appears cannot be treated directly as a sign that removal is complete.

There are two candidate approaches. The first is to add handling to the teardown branch whose name is the closest match. The advantage is that the changes stay localized; the drawback is that it may mistakenly attribute a state anomaly in the caller to a transport problem. The second is to first select a caller that still uses this action, record the version it uses, the entry point through which it enters removal, and the result at that time, then decide whether code near the entry point needs to change. Start with the second approach.

Do not include the adjacent cleanup on swarm in the pilot scope yet. That way, even if an anomaly appears, it can only show that the relationship between the selected caller and removal needs further investigation; it cannot establish that the teardown order for the entire swarm is wrong.

# peer removal trial plan

This plan is still being referenced because it preserves a starting point that is easy to fall back into: after seeing the name peer removal, it is natural to want to start making changes in nearby destruction or swarm branches. That approach was not entirely without value, but it once mistook "being able to find related literals" for "having identified the operation boundary". This review has not removed the old paragraphs; when investigating similar anomalies later, readers can still see here why the scope was made too broad at the time.

The only initial clue was `webtorrent.min.js`. The earlier investigation followed `peer`, `destroys`, `swarm`, `once`, and `once.` into the code. They came from the same local code-reading starting point: some terms were close to cleanup operations, while others were close to one-shot callbacks. The working assumption at the time was that, since these terms were clustered nearby, peer removal was likely a processing point that could be replaced independently.

> Old plan, preserving its original intent: first try a change in the destruction branch with the closest matching name; if the anomaly disappears, go back and verify the caller. swarm cleanup can be treated as an extension of the same issue, and `once` can initially be treated as completion of removal.

That assessment did not ultimately hold up as an actionable conclusion. Name matches only provide navigation, and cannot turn adjacent branches into a single operation. In particular, `once` only indicates that the local code contains a clue about a one-shot callback, and does not justify asserting that the peer has left, that state finalization is complete, or that the caller no longer holds any associated state. The old plan was therefore not turned into a change list; it remains here as a reminder to distinguish "call entry point", "actual version", and "current result" during review.

## Narrowing the focus during review

The symptom recorded in RLY-217 is an abnormal state after peer removal processing. The card's requirement for this page is narrow: find a caller that still uses "peer removal", and check its actual version, entry point, and current result. This requirement changed the trial sequence. The question is no longer "which cleanup point looks like removal", but "which still-running call chain brings removal into an abnormal state".

The dependency check already performed only shows that this card is relevant to the current verification, and does not establish that the anomaly has been reproduced or that any adjacent location in `webtorrent.min.js` should be modified. The earlier claim that the dependency check meant the issue had been located should be treated as outdated. It is retained because some people will jump directly from the card title to this plan; without making this correction explicit, readers could easily follow the old path and keep expanding the scope of changes.

Here, "caller" means a specific entry point that still uses this operation, not every module that can interact with a peer. Three items need to be recorded side by side: which actual version the caller is on; which entry point it uses to enter removal; what the current result is when observed. If any of the three is missing, the anomaly cannot be attributed back to transport cut, nor can it be attributed to swarm based on the name.

## Two approaches that can still be tried this time

**Probe using local literals.**

The first candidate is retained because it is inexpensive: starting in `webtorrent.min.js`, read through the areas near `peer`, `destroys`, and `swarm` one by one to check whether there is explicit removal handling. It is suitable for answering "what exactly did the old clues point to", not for serving directly as a fix path. If the probe only finds neighboring terms, neighboring callbacks, or similar names, stop there; these are findings from reading the code, not behavioral relationships.

The cost of this candidate is that local code can seem more important than the caller. For cumulative transport cut, this bias is particularly dangerous: a seemingly reasonable finalization adjustment may obscure the fact that the wrong version was selected for the caller, that the entry point has long since moved, or that the anomaly record does not describe the same removal at all. The old draft reduced these possibilities to "verify the caller again", understating their importance.

**Trace back from an entry point still in use.**

The second candidate remains the priority. First obtain a caller sample, then bring the version, entry point, and result back together in the same pass through the code. Only if the entry point actually reaches the relevant location in `webtorrent.min.js` should discussion continue on whether that location is a trial point; if the entry point does not reach it, the old investigation path still has reference value, but should not be used as the basis for implementation changes.

The benefit of this approach is not that it finds the code faster, but that it breaks "abnormal state" down into facts that can be assessed. The caller Fang Ke may already have a state discrepancy before removal, or the discrepancy may only arise after entry; the current material does not yet support choosing between the two. Conflating these two cases as a peer removal issue would make any subsequent observation look like support for the old hypothesis.

## The third approach was not chosen at the time

Including all handling adjacent to swarm cleanup in the cut was considered, on the grounds that it would save one round trip. This approach was not taken into the trial. It bundles handling from different entry points and versions into a single change package, making it impossible, if something goes wrong, to tell which location changed the state or which location should be rolled back. Because the existing records do not provide the complete call relationships, this plan is retained only as an approach that was not adopted.

`once` is not treated as a decision point either. A one-shot callback is worth marking while reading because it may help explain the control flow; but it cannot replace the caller's result. The old draft used it as an approximation of "removal complete", which is no longer applicable. If an actual entry-point sample later links the callback to the state change in removal, that relationship should be recorded separately, rather than backfilled as a premise that this plan had already confirmed.

## Trial scope and stopping points

This round permits only two kinds of work: identify a caller that still uses peer removal; record that caller's version, entry point, and current result side by side. Code reading can start at `webtorrent.min.js`, but finding `destroys` or `swarm` must not automatically expand the scope to all cleanup branches.

The idea of a local change should be withdrawn in the following cases: the caller's version differs from the code being read; the entry point does not reach the location under investigation; or the result does not establish whether the anomaly occurred before or after removal. Withdrawing does not mean declaring RLY-217 irrelevant, but rather no longer treating this old path as the implementation target and returning to the caller sample for further checking.

If all three pieces of information are available, the next step is still not to merge changes immediately, but to ask another, narrower question: whether the abnormal state can still be observed after this entry point enters removal. Only once there is clear evidence on this question is it worth deciding whether the trial point should be on the entry-point side or the adjacent cleanup side. The current plan does not have that evidence.

## Notes for future readers

`webtorrent.min.js` remains a useful starting point for verification because the old records did reach this location from the issue name and call name; it is not proof that peer removal belongs here. RLY-217 also serves only as navigation for cross-checking the anomaly against the caller, not as a substitute for checking the actual version.

Open questions remain: which caller still retains this path; what its actual version is; on which side of removal the state anomaly first becomes visible. The old draft proposed "change first, verify later", while this review changes that to "verify one entry point first, then decide whether to try a change". This narrows the plan while retaining its limitations as a record of the old cut.

# Caller integration testing proposal — not adopted

This proposal stopped at the comparison stage, while license-client-integration was still unresolved. The entry-point material available at the time was in `docs/adj-license/proposals/not-adopted-LICENSE-client-integration-approach.md`; it put client and extension in the same integration testing scope, but did not provide a unified integration approach that could serve as a direct replacement. This page preserves an approach that was not pursued at the time; it should not be used to infer that later implementations adopted or ruled out any of these entry points.

## Alternatives at the time

One option was to continue organizing calls around `reqq`. The benefit was that the existing entry points would not have to be split apart immediately, and changes during integration testing could stay close to the existing paths. The issue was not the name, but the failure exit paths: the two records in the material did not describe the same exit scenario. Continuing to treat them as one call chain would leave callers unsure whether to retry the original entry point after a failure or switch to another adapter layer.

Another option was to split `peer` out on its own. The aim was to keep the different failure exit paths with their respective objects, so that `reqq` would not have to carry two different recovery semantics. The cost was an extra entry point for the client to recognize; if extension still integrated under the old assumptions, the split would only defer the decision, not remove the ambiguity in integration testing.

At the time, the preference was to try the latter first, but a preference was not a decision. The material did not say whether splitting out `peer` would cover existing callers, nor did it establish that the old entry point could be retained in every failure scenario. This route was therefore not recorded as an agreed change or made a release prerequisite.

## Proposed trial scope

The trial would compare only how the two entry points express failure exit paths, without expanding into a caller rewrite. Retain `reqq` as the baseline; `peer` is to handle only the segment that could be clearly distinguished in the original records. Integration testing would need to confirm whether the same client would get two incompatible exit behaviors depending on the entry point. If choosing an entry point still required guesswork in an outer layer, the split would not be viable.

`stream` was the only caller in use explicitly recorded at the time, but its verification was incomplete. It could count neither as a sample supporting the split nor as evidence against it. The integration status of ESM was also only noted alongside the material, without an actionable conclusion; do not infer from these two unfinished items that the adapter layer already had fixed boundaries.

## If the approach is dropped

The rollback conditions were simple: `peer` could not clearly distinguish the two failure exit paths, or callers had to retain both sets of decision logic to keep working. If either condition occurred, stop the split trial and restore the single-entry-point assumption for `reqq`; whether to restore only the old entry point or also remove adapter code added during the trial was not decided at the time.

Later integration test results have not been added to this page. When revisiting it, first open the material above and confirm the actual call sites for `stream`, then decide whether to write a new proposal; do not backfill later status as though it were a trial conclusion already reached here.
