# Current and Legacy Entry Point Migration Index

`docs/adj-license/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md` is now a migration ledger. It records the legacy entry points still found in license-client-integration, replacement locations currently being trialed, and client and extension consumers that have not yet left the compatibility paths. This index does not order entry points by the directory tree, nor does it connect two labels into a call chain just because they appear in the same sample.

In this index, a "current entry point" is the location that a particular batch of consumers actually enters at present; a "legacy entry point" is a location that this batch still needs to retain, can still query, or can still restore. These are not fixed roles encoded in filenames. One consumer having moved to a replacement location does not mean another consumer has also completed migration. When no material is available to check, keep the original description marked as outdated rather than filling it in with a similarly named page.

The specific objects currently retained are as follows:

| Object | Position in the index | Current handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `torrent` | Legacy path candidate compared in the first version | Keep it in its original batch; do not declare it retired on this basis |
| `piece` | Replacement location that the first version leaned toward splitting out | Only allow it to be trialed by a single consumer |
| `wire` | Trial track name in subsequent records | Return to that consumer's legacy entry point if inconsistencies arise |
| `worker` | Caller in current use that had not been verified at the time | Do not expand the migration scope until the inventory is complete |
| `callback`, `stream`, `peer` | Labels in specific call samples | Keep each with its original sample; do not infer upstream or downstream relationships |

These labels serve only to help readers return to the original samples. They cannot replace the actual names of a client or extension, nor can they be assembled into a path that appears complete but has not actually been verified.

## Create a Batch Record First

Before starting, begin with an actual consumer. Record the entry point that consumer currently uses, the replacement location to be trialed, the original input, the version, and the first result. Write separate records for client and extension; if the same consumer retains both a legacy entry point and a replacement location, record them separately as well, rather than collapsing the two states into "migrated".

Add to the index in the following order, rather than filling every blank first:

```text
Consumer: the actual client or extension observed
Legacy entry point: the original call location for this batch
Replacement location: the location being trialed for this batch
Input and version: keep unchanged
First result: success, error, or stopped at a specific step
Second call: the state after calling again through the same entry point
Rollback record: whether the legacy entry point was restored, and the separate result after restoration
```

These are not new field names. Retain whatever names the existing samples in the index use; write unconfirmed wherever there is no name. The original input and first result must sit directly beside this batch's entry point record; do not retain only cleaned-up screenshots or the final green status. If new evidence is added later, append it after the original batch rather than rewriting the first failure as "normal afterward".

Change only one condition within a batch: switch the entry point from the legacy location to the replacement location, while keeping the input and version unchanged. Only then can differences in the replacement location itself be distinguished from differences caused by changes to the input or version. Retain the second call as well, because opening the entry point for the first time is not the same as the state after reaching the result.

## Two Types of Failure Already Encountered

The behavior recorded in RLYA-006 is: when entering the exit entry point through the normal entry point, the second step is rejected. Record which step was rejected rather than shortening this to "the entry point will not open". Being able to open the normal entry point through the first step is not enough to show that the migrated path works; conversely, failure at the second step should not erase the fact that the entry point was reachable.

RLYA-010 describes a different type of behavior: the exit entry point opens, but it keeps spinning at the current result. This sample must not be merged with the previous one. The key point in the former is where the rejection occurs; in the latter, it is that the current result has not returned. Both require the entry point state and subsequent state to be written separately in the batch record. Checking only the home page or only the first opening will obscure the distinction between these two problems, treating both as the same "migration incomplete" issue.

Therefore, a batch record must distinguish at least three stages: whether the entry point was entered, whether the current result was reached, and whether the second call still produced the same type of state. If a failure occurs at a later location such as `callback`, mark it only beside that sample; do not use it to classify all consumers labeled `callback` as having the same fault.

RLYA-010 also requires the time of the current entry point change to be marked beside the trend. Statistics from before and after the change cannot be directly subtracted, because the entry point state may differ on the two sides. The index does not need to provide a trend conclusion for the entire batch; it only needs to let reviewers see that this statistical period spans an entry point change and know that the two ends cannot be directly compared.

## User View and Internal Records

The alignment work in RLYA-019 requires reading results through the normal user entry point, then recording the time difference using separate columns for those results and the raw internal events. Keep these two columns under the same batch in the index, but do not merge them into a single timeline. The result visible through the normal user entry point is the state the consumer actually experiences; the raw internal events are simply another record. A difference in their order of appearance does not automatically mean either side is wrong.

This distinction is especially important during migration trials. An internal event appearing does not mean the normal entry point has completed; a normal entry point returning does not mean the internal records have synchronized. If only one column can be obtained, record what is available in that column and mark the other as unverified. Do not use internal records to provide confirmation on behalf of normal consumers, and do not infer unseen internal details from the user view.

The rejection at the second step described in RLYA-006 should be assigned to the specific step in the normal entry point column. The continuous spinning described in RLYA-010 belongs at the current result location. This allows a later review to distinguish entry point permissions, waiting for a result, and a lack of alignment between the two sets of records, rather than yielding a generic "legacy entry point migration issue".

## When a Sampling Toggle Change Spans Batches

For batches involving the license-client-integration sampling toggle, first confirm the toggle state at the original time of migration. The constraint in RLYA-015 is to start a separate segment for data after the toggle was enabled, rather than backfilling results from before it was enabled into the same batch. The index should note whether the toggle change applied to the legacy entry point, the replacement location, or a bypass call; if material from the original time is unavailable, record only that the toggle state is unconfirmed.

Records from before and after the toggle change must not be mixed when evaluating the replacement location. They can provide additional evidence of whether a particular call left an internal record, but cannot replace actual confirmation from the client or extension. If both the entry point and the toggle were changed during the trial, keep it in trial status: when the available material cannot separate the two changes, do not expand to the next batch of consumers.

Retaining "start a separate segment" here is more useful than adding an aggregate number. It lets later readers see when the data began to reflect conditions with the toggle enabled, and prevents the unsampled gap in the preceding segment from being misread as an absence of calls to the replacement entry point.

## Batch Progression and Stopping Points

Begin progression with actual consumers for which both the legacy entry point and the replacement location can be identified. After completing a batch, update only three items for that batch: the entry point actually used, the result at the replacement location, and where historical queries should still begin. Review the next batch against these objects; do not insert similarly named items discovered later directly into completed batches.

For the window with no records in RLYA-006, first ask the person on duty to verify the current revision; when there are no records, write cannot determine in the index. This gap cannot be filled by a single attempt through the normal entry point. Likewise, the change time in RLYA-010 applies only to the corresponding trend; do not extend it into a change that occurred for all callers.

If any of the following remains unconfirmed, keep this batch in trial status:

- The replacement location does not yet have a corresponding result from an actual consumer;
- The starting point for historical queries through the legacy entry point is unclear;
- The failure is recorded only as "unavailable", without locating it at the entry point, current result, or a subsequent location;
- The normal user view and raw internal events are mixed into a single timeline;
- Data from before and after the sampling toggle change is treated as one segment;
- `worker` is still only a caller name awaiting verification.

Write the stopping point beside that batch. The index as a whole should continue to retain the states of other batches; do not mark all callers as failed because one batch is blocked, or retire all legacy entry points because one batch succeeds.

# Release Automation Status Inconsistency Postmortem

This incident occurred between .github/workflows and the build queue formed by release. The same release object showed two statuses in succession at the current entry; selection did not match the old record, and the current revision reported by the two entry points also differed. No direct subtraction was made between the before-and-after counts at the time; the original record and recovery page were both retained in their respective locations.

The initial assessment was that selection had read an old record. We then tried retrying through the entry point used at the time, but the status did not converge, and retries were stopped. At the second check, the only thing that could be confirmed was that the current entry point could still return content; its revision differed from the one seen the first time, and nothing was recorded about what happened during the missing interval.

The main impact was on the release decision: the build queue cannot determine that the artifact is usable based only on the last green output line, and the withdrawal window cannot be closed on that basis either. The ESM path could be recovered at the time, so the record at one point attributed the problem to the request side; that attribution is retained here, but do not later use it to infer that the queue was operating normally.

During the on-call shift, a segment of request context was extracted. No normalization was performed at the junction between the end of the seed address and the file path, leaving `/seed//file.bin` in the output. The same excerpt also contained these symbols:

```js
_getMaxOutstandingRequests()
_hasAllPieces()
_hasNoPieces()
_storeCacheSlots()
_isIPv4()
```

At the time, they were treated as signs that the request branch had reached the expected point; in retrospect, this only shows that these call names appeared in the record and cannot explain why the two statuses coexisted. Another queue excerpt listed rate limiting and stream state side by side: `_downloadLimit`, `_uploadLimit`, `_fileStreams`, `throttleDownload`. The worker side left `loadWorker`, `workerPortCount`, and `enableSecure`, with no corresponding completion record.

After the recovery page confirmed that ESM was available, the retry scope was not expanded further. "The request has recovered, so release will correct itself" in the original record is old wording, retained for anyone who needs to verify the handling at the time. Why reqq changed, whether there was an unrecorded switch between the two revisions, and whether the withdrawal window was affected by that switch all remain unconfirmed.

For exit-window materials, start at `docs/adj-file-storage/release/file-storage-release-automation-exit-window-checklist.md` as before. Two rules from the old version are retained here to help interpret the early records: do not clean up after seeing `uTP`; stop if `torrent` has not appeared. At the time, "execution record gaps" and "the page's last value" were not handled separately, making it easy in later reviews to mistake a normal result from a neighboring entry for completion of this entry. Do not use these two rules as the sole basis for decisions now.

RLYC-002 made this gap explicit: the neighboring entries' results at that point were normal, but this entry cut off before the execution record. The page's final value is only corroborating evidence; it cannot fill in actions that were not recorded in between. The handling in RLYC-009 also narrowed post-recovery observation to a single entry point: starting at the point of recovery, take only the first record; do not overwrite it with later summaries at this stage. RLYC-016 adds another constraint: use alert receipt records to determine whether alerts were silenced during the window; if there are no alert receipt records, do not write "recovered".

## Record evidence in this order when closing the window

1. **Establish the window boundaries first.**

   - [ ] Open the checklist referenced above and find `metadata` near this exit action, along with the last visible result.
   - [ ] Keep records in their original chronological order. If the sequence on the page does not match the current revision, reorder it by the original times first; retain the page's final value only as corroborating evidence.
   - [ ] List any build queue entries still associated with this window beneath the exit action. Not seeing later entries does not mean the queue has emptied; write only "not seen" here.

   The purpose here is not to copy out every artifact version. Before exiting, you need to know which records have appeared, which records cut off and where, and which action the last directly visible result belongs to. If the original order cannot be restored, stop closing the window and preserve the state; do not substitute a cleaned-up summary for the original sequence.

2. **Check execution records separately.**

   - [ ] Do not fill in this entry's execution result using a normal result from a neighboring entry.
   - [ ] If the exit action is followed directly by the page's final value, mark it "execution record not seen".
   - [ ] If there are multiple versions or signs of withdrawal among the records, retain only the content directly adjacent to this window; leave the rest on the original page and do not guess at the sequence here.

   In the old checklist, "the last visible result" was often treated as a signal that closeout could proceed directly. Now use it only as a reference point: it shows how far you have read, not that the actions in between necessarily completed. If an execution record is missing, keep the exit window open while waiting for the original records to be filled in or for the owner to explicitly take over.

3. **On recovery, do not backfill with later summaries.**

   - [ ] Start at the point of recovery and find the first record.
   - [ ] Place it alongside the last pre-exit result; do not write later summary text back into the recovery point.
   - [ ] If the first record is still inconclusive, write "first post-recovery record unconfirmed" and stop drawing further conclusions.

   This avoids attaching a later green result to the recovery action. There may be other builds or artifact versions after recovery; attributing them to this exit is outside this checklist's scope. If further work is needed, just leave the original path and the location of the gap.

   - [ ] If alert receipt records exist, write only the status they actually show.
   - [ ] If there are no alert receipt records, leave the gap; do not fill in a recovery on that basis or use the absence of alerts as proof of normal operation.

   Silencing alerts and completing the release are not the same thing. Silencing only affects whether anomalies could be seen in the alert receipt records at the time; it cannot replace execution records or the owner's release sign-off.

5. **Decide whether to stop or exit.**

   - [ ] If the original chronological order, execution records, first post-recovery record, and alert receipt records all line up, record the exit action and the last visible result.

# File Release Automation Split Proposal

This comparison starts with the two failure exits in `docs/adj-file-storage/proposals/not-adopted-File-and-chunk-storage-release-automation-approach.md`. Previously, `DHT` and `web seed` were grouped in a single release decision, which was easier to read but made it unclear when something went wrong whether the seed address, file path, or release entry point itself had sent the request off course.

The advantage of keeping the `DHT` route is that we don't have to move the existing selection entry point; the cost is that web seed errors will still be grouped in the same place. Splitting out web seed keeps file path concatenation and release selection in an independent branch, but requires us to specify which entry point to restore when backing out; we can't treat the two as equivalent just because both can retrieve the file.

## Proposed Trial Approach

The web seed branch accepts only file paths relative to the torrent root directory, then appends them to the seed URL. The path-boundary sample should be kept as `/seed//file.bin`; don't normalize it away in the release layer first. This double slash is part of the concatenated result; retaining it allows subsequent request behavior to be compared with the old entry point.

The download and upload limits remain `_downloadLimit` and `_uploadLimit`, respectively; choosing web seed must not bypass `throttleDownload`. File streams continue to be managed by `_fileStreams`, and cache slots still use `_storeCacheSlots`; the concurrency cap follows the existing result from `_getMaxOutstandingRequests`, with no separate release-specific value introduced as part of this approach.

Completion status is not inferred from the release script either. `_hasNoPieces` and `_hasAllPieces` remain the same decision points; web seed only affects the request source, not their results. If a worker is needed, the loading order for `loadWorker` remains unchanged, and no separate port count is created for `workerPortCount` as a result of the split; `enableSecure` and `_isIPv4` also remain in the existing address and connection branches.

The case against splitting is not weak: a single entry point at least prevents two sets of release actions from each accumulating their own exceptions. This proposal leans toward splitting because the two failure exits in the available material already differ; keeping a shared entry point would just force us to guess the path first during troubleshooting. This assessment has not yet covered the existing callers of `wire`, so this is not presented as a change already in effect.

## Backout Points

Before the trial, first confirm that reproduction is possible through the public entry point along the original file-storage-release-automation path; single-machine results can only help with diagnosis. If the failure exits for the web seed branch and the DHT entry point cannot be distinguished, or if, after the switch, file streams and cache slots no longer converge where they did before, back out of this split approach.

Whether backing out should restore only the old entry point is still undecided. If the trial has introduced additional branches for the worker or secure connections, restoring the entry point alone would leave a partial selection state behind; if neither has changed, a full rollback might instead broaden the impact. We need to check the callers of `wire` first, then decide the scope of the backout.

versions.body:
# ESM Cutover Decision Record

The draft left a very short wrap-up: torrent-state entry retained, transport window not carried forward. It described the submission boundary at the time, but compressed two different judgments into one sentence. When this record was reviewed later, the sentence was read as "the window plan had already been rejected," and some also read it as "the existing entry had already been chosen as the long-term path." Both readings are broader than the original decision.

This page preserves the time context of that ESM cutover review at Northstar Relay Systems. It is not a general account of all later transport changes. The goal at the time was deliberately narrow: do not let the module-form switch also turn a state window that had not yet been clearly explained into an established change. The draft's conclusion remains valid, but it covers only the ordering of choices in that round.

## Tradeoffs Left by the Draft

There were two paths on the review table.

The first was to continue using the current torrent-state entry point. It was not inherently more suitable because it was "old" or "new"; it was adopted at the time because existing checks could obtain the transport state presented by the node from here. The ESM cutover could be discussed around what was already visible, without first changing where the state was observed.

The second was to adjust the transport window in sync with the cutover. This idea was not an incidental cleanup item. Its supporters wanted to organize the state boundary at the same time, avoiding the need to return to an adjacent location later for another explanation. The problem was that the existing material did not explain how maintainers should interpret the same transport state after the window changed, nor did it establish a reference relationship between the old window and the proposed window.

Therefore, the decision at the time was not to choose a winner between two permanent plans, but to sequence them within the scope that could be submitted. The ESM changes supported by the existing observation material went first; the window's interpretation was left separately in the record. This ordering was a review decision, not a technical rejection of the window object.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[torrent-state entry point] --> B[ESM cutover]
  A --> C[raw node output]
  B --> D[Proposed change]
  C --- D
  E[transport window adjustment] --> F[Reservation]
```

The connecting lines in the diagram represent only the relationships among objects that were kept side by side in the discussion at the time. The raw node output and the proposed change were placed together; this does not mean that the output itself made the decision for the maintainer. The window adjustment points to a reservation; this also does not mean it was deleted. It simply was not included in that submission.

## What the Review Required to Remain

The exact wording in the meeting materials was: `keep the raw node output beside the proposed change`. The word beside is important here. The output records the state actually presented by the node during the check; the proposed change records the interpretation and action that maintainers were preparing to take based on it. Writing them as one smooth explanation would make it difficult for later readers to distinguish which sentence was an observation and which was a judgment.

Another working constraint was adopted at the time: `Start from a reproducible repository path and separate observed transport state from the explanation a maintainer is proposing.` It was not a process name that had to be applied to every change, but a way to resolve the specific confusion in this discussion. Some people obtained the state and then discussed the window directly; others first discussed what they wanted to change and then went back to fill in the state. Both styles caused the original observation and its interpretation to overlap.

Starting from a reproducible repository path at least lets readers know where the state was obtained. Separating the state from the interpretation lets readers know that a change did not gain more support merely because the wording was complete. The scope approved by the review extended only as far as the existing material covered; an inference without corresponding output remained only a reservation.

The draft described this as "the node output makes the initial judgment." This wording is not accurate in retrospect, so its origin is retained but it is no longer used. Node output does not make judgments. It is observation material. The judgment comes from the review's decision about what the material can and cannot establish. If the output is called a judgment, readers can easily treat a single node state as the reason the window adjustment has already been established.

## Decision Made

This round's decision had three parts.

First, the current torrent-state entry point would continue to serve as the observation point for the ESM cutover. "Continue" here only means that this round did not replace the observation point with part of the window plan; it did not declare that entry to be the sole state entry going forward.

Second, the transport window adjustment would not enter this round's ESM change. It was not listed as prohibited, nor was it ruled not worth doing. It simply did not have explanatory material commensurate with this round's change. Recasting "the material was insufficient to include it in this submission" as "it has been proven impossible to adjust" would change the nature of the original decision.

Third, the corresponding raw node output should remain beside the proposed change. This was not meant to treat a piece of output as a decorative attachment. Readers should be able to see both the transport state presented by the node and how the maintainer will interpret that state. The two can be checked against each other, but they cannot replace each other.

Together, these three parts define only the submission boundary for the ESM cutover: retain the existing observation point first, advance the changes that can already be explained, and leave the window discussion in a position where it can be reopened. The draft did not separate the "boundary for this round" from the "long-term direction," which is exactly why this addendum was needed later.

## Why the Window Adjustment Was Not Included

The main cost of the window plan was not that it changed one more thing, but that it changed both the observation context and the object being interpreted. If the window were changed first and readers were then asked to interpret the original state using the new view, they would face a question that had no answer at the time: does the transport state being seen belong to the old window, the proposed window, or the result of comparing the two?

The existing raw node output could answer only a narrow question: what state the node presented at the time under the selected path. It could not automatically answer whether the window should be expanded, contracted, or moved. Nor could it explain whether the same state should still be interpreted in the same way after the window changed. Folding these additional judgments into the ESM cutover would make the submission appear complete while actually removing its clear reference point.

Another approach was to omit the window discussion entirely and leave only the conclusion "entry retained." This was not adopted either. It would erase the costs that had already been raised, causing anyone who reopened the window plan later to assume that it had never been discussed. This is exactly what the reservation is for: it is neither approval nor rejection, but a way to keep the observation and interpretation that have not yet been connected in the same decision.

At the time, some people favored adjusting the window first and then adding a new state explanation. That sequence did not enter the decision because it changed the observation context first and then asked readers to go back and understand the old state. Others favored removing the window from the record entirely so that the ESM discussion would not continue to expand. That approach also did not enter the decision because it would cause the next round to lose the context for why the issue had been paused.

Therefore, this record retains both the approved narrow scope and the unapproved window idea. The former shows what could be submitted at that time; the latter shows that what was missing was not willingness, but material connecting the observed state with the maintainer's interpretation.

## Corrections After Review

The draft's "current entry retained" was once treated as an endorsement of the old entry. Correction: it was only the minimum choice for that ESM cutover. If transport state is observed from a different location later, the old output can serve only as a reference for what was observed then; it cannot directly become the basis for the new observation location. Even if the same entry point is still used, the record should again explain which part of the state the proposed change interprets, rather than applying this conclusion directly.

The draft also did not make the scope of raw clear. What must be retained here is the juxtaposition of the raw node output and the proposed change, not merely pasting a piece of output and considering the review complete. The output must make clear which change it corresponds to; the change also cannot merely cite the output while omitting its own interpretation. The two types of material each have their own purpose. Mixing them makes it impossible for later readers to determine whether the disagreement is about the observation or the interpretation.

This review did not re-decide the transport window. It corrected only two overly strong readings: retaining the entry does not mean long-term designation, and deferring the window does not mean the plan was rejected. The old short conclusion remains in the version history because it accurately records the submission action at the time; the added text merely restores the qualification that it originally left unstated.

## Notes for Follow-up

The handoff for the peer transport window cutover was later recorded separately in DOC-44. This page preserves only the relationship between the two pieces of material: the window issue was not resolved together with the ESM submission in this round. DOC-44 is not an evidence patch for this decision, nor should it be used retroactively to change the boundary judgment made here at the time.

If the window plan enters review again, first confirm whether the new observation path is still in the same context as the old output. If it is not, obtain the state again and explain how the proposed change interprets it. If it is, the old decision still cannot simply be cited, because it records the tradeoff at one cutover, not a long-term rule applicable to all transport adjustments.

This record is still dated in places. "Current entry" refers to the torrent-state entry discussed at the time; it does not guarantee that it is equivalent to the entry used during later maintenance. Retaining this somewhat inaccurate temporal reference better fits the record's original purpose than turning the old decision into a general-purpose guide.

# Store factory callback entry-point trace

The previous draft treated store-factory as a name to look for. After review, this name is better used as a route marker: the person taking over should start from the repository's public entry point and follow a single direct call that is already visible, rather than jumping by name among storage-related files. Following that path to the callback audit leaves a trace that can be reviewed, not a string of potentially relevant search results.

The starting point remains `webtorrent.min.js`. This condensed form isn't suitable for breaking nearby symbols into a module map; during review, just treat locations where store, storage, callback, and run appear as return points. First determine which handoff in the public entry point contains store-factory, then look one layer up for the layer that passes it in or invokes it. Here, a direct caller means the call layer immediately reachable from the current call site, not a branch in the same file that happens to contain the same word.

This is the line used for the actual review:

```text
Repository public entry point
    |
    v
store-factory
    |
    v
Direct caller
    |
    v
storage callback audit
    |
    v
First actual consumer
```

The arrows in the diagram represent the call relationships being checked in this review, not the directory hierarchy. The store-factory side is responsible for taking the review toward storage; the direct caller is the key to narrowing the scope; and storage callback audit is where we determine whether the callback is merely mentioned or has actually been received. The trace on this page ends once it reaches the first actual consumer. Any later processing does not change this entry path and should not be added to make a complete chain.

The review record does not need to quote large sections around the compressed file. Each trace-back should leave four things: the handoff in the public entry point where store-factory appears; one direct caller confirmed by following downward from that point; the corresponding storage callback audit within that call line; and the location where the callback is first actually received. The first two prevent entry-point drift, while the latter two show that the audit has moved beyond the name or comment layer. If any one item can only be filled in through a same-name search, leave it blank rather than writing the search hit onto the arrow.

The direct-caller field must not be omitted. If only the factory name is written, later readers will pick one of storage, store, or callback and continue searching, so the review scope quickly fans out again. Once the direct caller is fixed, the scope for assessing callback audit narrows to one known handoff; adjacent storage snippets can help identify it, but a relationship not connected from that call site cannot replace this hop. This ordering is also what this review added relative to the first draft.

The thing people tend to skip during a trace-back isn't store-factory, but the word "audit." It may lead people to look first for same-named files, comments, or check fragments; those locations can help identify the term, but they cannot prove that the callback has arrived from the current call site. The actual order should be reversed: first use store-factory to fix one direct caller, then confirm storage callback audit along this line, and finally inspect the first place that actually receives the callback. If the search expands by name first, it usually produces several fragments that all look like entry points, making it hard to explain which one is connected to the public entry point.

The release CI run stays beside this line rather than in the middle of the arrows. It is useful during review for confirming the materials consulted and the runtime context at the time, and for helping later readers return to the same check; but the run itself does not create a call edge. If a fragment pointed to by a run differs from the same-named fragment visible in the current file, use the direct relationship established by following down from the entry point as the basis, then record the difference in a side note on the run. The side note should only identify which section it helped locate; do not write it as evidence that the callback was consumed.

This review closes the gap where only the factory name was known and the next hop was not: after store-factory, keep one direct caller first, then follow the line to the first actual consumer of storage callback audit. Here, "actual consumer" refers only to the first location on this review path that needs to process the callback; it does not extend to a description of all subsequent storage behavior. If there are multiple adjacent processing points after the first consumption, they do not need to be laid out here; this page should retain the entry into audit, not a checklist of storage-side processing.

There is still one place where the trace should stop: if answering what comes after the first consumer requires another owner, state at the handoff point that the current trace has reached the first consumption point after callback audit, and hand off the question together with this path. The question should focus on what the processing after this consumer means, not broadly ask about storage as a whole. Also, just because ownership of what follows is unclear, do not go back and put same-named files with no call edge into the path. The entry left this way is sufficient for the next audit and will not misdocument the route marker as an implementation.

versions.body:
# Worker cancellation watch discrepancy postmortem

During one worker cancellation watch window, the monitoring side did not see results appear as originally planned. The team did not interpret this discrepancy as a failure of the cancellation operation itself: what was visible at the time was a mismatch between the plan and the results, and the cause was still unresolved.

## Timeline

- When the discrepancy was first noticed, the window was still under observation. The visible state originally used to confirm the cancellation result did not line up; continuing to judge results under the original plan would mix this discrepancy into the assessment.
- The investigation first preserved the package manifest diff from that time. The older notes tended to treat this diff and the anomaly as part of the same line of investigation; this explained why a base-version comparison was needed, but did not establish that the diff was the cause.
- A temporary recovery followed so observation would not have to remain stuck on that anomalous window. The recovery only addressed the need to continue observation during that shift; it did not provide a root cause for worker cancellation or confirm whether it would recur under the same conditions.
- Review added a control: separate a base regression from a newly covered behavior. In other words, first distinguish the base regression from the behavior newly covered this time. They must not be treated as a single issue just because both appeared around the diff.

## Impact and assessment at the time

This discrepancy affected interpretation of the watch window; it was not a confirmed finding of a transport failure. The team therefore could not use that window as evidence that "the cancellation behavior has been verified as planned." Continued observation after the temporary recovery could only show that the window could continue to be used; it could not be used to infer that the cause was already known at the time of recovery.

Retain the original working assessment: the package manifest diff was worth investigating, and the base regression needed to be kept separate. When cited later, this assessment was easy to read as "the diff had pinpointed the anomaly." The investigation had not actually reached that point; it was only the starting point at the time.

Still unanswered: what directly triggered the visible results to diverge from the original plan; whether the effects of the base regression and the newly covered behavior on the window can be separated; and whether the temporary recovery masked a condition that appeared only during that watch period. If a similar discrepancy occurs again, the diff and window observations from that occurrence should be preserved first, before deciding whether to pursue the same line of investigation.
